author: Mark Manson
description:
Being honest doesn’t mean saying every true thing the moment you think it. If the other person isn’t ready to hear it, or the truth would only cause pain without telling them anything useful, it can do as much damage as staying quiet.

Research even shows that small, kind lies told for someone’s benefit can increase trust, even when the person knows you’re doing it. And if “I’m just being honest” is your go-to defense, it might be worth asking whether you’re being honest or just being an asshole.
title: When Telling the Truth Does More Harm Than Good

author: Mark Manson
description:
John Stuart Mill was raised to be a happiness machine. His father had him learning Greek at three and Latin at eight, every hour of his childhood planned so he'd grow into the happiest, most useful man possible.

At twenty, he fell apart. Nothing brought him joy. Every pleasure felt hollow.

Years later he summed up what went wrong in one line: "Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so."

Relationships run into the same wall. Once you start auditing how happy you are with someone, a slow Sunday turns into evidence. A short text gets reread four times.

The research on couples points somewhere pretty boring. One study found that how long people had been together, or whether they were married, didn't predict their happiness. How satisfied they felt in the connection did.

You can't inspect your way into satisfied. It builds up in the moments you stop checking.

title: Stop Trying to Be Happy

author: Mark Manson
description:
Back in the '70s there was a woman who couldn't wear a necklace. The weight of it on her collarbone reminded her of a snake, and she'd spent her entire adult life dodging snakes.

Then she had one afternoon with Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura. By the time she left, she had a snake in her lap.

OK, phobia cured. That's not the interesting part.

Bandura checked back in six months later. The fear was gone. But his participants were also speaking up at work. Asking for raises. Having fights they'd put off for years. Sticking to diets they'd quit.

And the necklace lady? Wearing necklaces.

They walked out of that room with one new fact about themselves, and it started poking holes in other limits they'd assumed were permanent.

Bandura built his most influential paper on it. Whether you'll take on something hard has very little to do with how you feel about yourself. It comes down to whether you've got evidence you can pull it off.
